# 2026 Spanish Grand Prix (Madring) — pre-race forecast

Round 14 of the 2026 world championship, Sunday 13 September, 57 laps of the new 5.414 km IFEMA Madrid circuit. Forecast is after qualifying and grid penalties, before the race.

## Grid (after penalties)

1 Norris (McLaren) 1:31.824  
2 Antonelli (Mercedes) +0.011  
3 Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.140  
4 Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.189  
5 Leclerc (Ferrari) +0.195  
6 Russell (Mercedes) +0.325  
7 Piastri (McLaren) +0.470  
8 Lawson (Red Bull) +0.492  
9 Colapinto (Alpine) +1.079  
10 Lindblad (Racing Bulls) +1.217  
11 Hulkenberg (Audi)  
12 Bortoleto (Audi)  
13 Ocon (Haas)  
14 Gasly (Alpine)  
15 Tsunoda (Racing Bulls)  
16 Albon (Williams)  
17 Alonso (Aston Martin)  
18 Perez (Cadillac)  
19 Bottas (Cadillac)  
20 Sainz (Williams, 3-place penalty for impeding Bottas)  
21 Bearman (Haas, no Q time after FP3 crash)  
22 Stroll (Aston Martin, 40-place PU penalty; no Q time)

Hadjar sits out a third race with a wrist injury; Lawson remains in the Red Bull, Tsunoda in the Racing Bulls.

## Championship and form

After 13 races (Monza): Antonelli 267, Russell 201, Hamilton 191, Norris 171, Leclerc 155, Verstappen 127, Piastri 116. Mercedes 468–346 over Ferrari in constructors.

Antonelli has seven wins including a 19th-to-first recovery at Monza last weekend. Mercedes swept practice here (Russell FP1, Antonelli FP2/FP3). Norris has won two of the last three Grands Prix (Hungary, Zandvoort) and produced what he called one of his best laps for pole. Ferrari have been Mercedes’ closest match on Friday/Saturday long-run and one-lap pace. Red Bull are a step behind the top three teams; Verstappen still extracted P3. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls occupy the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston Martin’s Honda package has been a reliability and speed disaster; Cadillac (Ferrari customer PU) has 0 points in 13 races.

## Circuit and race character

Madring is a first-time hybrid street/permanent layout: 22 corners, ~340 km/h on the straights, 24% banked “La Monumental”. F3 testing produced 19 red flags. Verstappen and Williams called it a potential “car killer”. Drivers (Antonelli, Russell, Hamilton, Alpine) all said on-track passing is painful — Antonelli spent two practice laps stuck behind a Williams. The run to Turn 1 is only ~200 m, so the start is bunched rather than a long drag.

Weather: dry, air high-20s/low-30s °C, track into the 50s. No rain. Pirelli C2/C3/C4; one-stop medium–hard is the natural call because pit loss plus hard passing punish an extra stop, though Friday graining and a two-stop (M–H–H) remain live. Norris/Antonelli/Verstappen/Russell/Piastri have no new softs; Hamilton and Leclerc kept a fresh C4 as a start/undercut wildcard. Safety-car market was heavily “yes” (~73%).

## Model

120k-race Monte Carlo with:

- Qualifying grid after penalties, plus a small T1 launch mix (Ferrari’s new-soft option, Verstappen’s starts, short run to T1).
- Two finishing-order regimes: a **processional** Plackett–Luce (track position dominates, matching driver feedback) and a **chaos** regime (multiple SCs / red flag / pit lottery) in which Mercedes race pace can still come through, as at Monza.
- Driver-specific mechanical and wall-incident hazards, elevated versus a mature permanent circuit. Extra DNS risk for Bearman (impact-structure rebuild) and Stroll (fresh Honda PU that already leaked water). Small DSQ risk, slightly higher at the front because of plank/skid wear on the banking.
- 90% rule: most DNFs are NC; a minority of late stoppages still classify.

Win probabilities are close to the post-quali market (Antonelli ≈ Norris, then Verstappen, then the Ferraris) but give Russell more win chance than the +2200 board, because the W17 is still the best race car and one SC cycle is enough to use it.

## Headline probabilities

| Driver | P(win) | P(podium) | P(top 10) | P(retirement) |
|--------|--------|-----------|-----------|----------------|
| Antonelli | 36.5% | 79.5% | 89.0% | 10.0% |
| Norris | 33.9% | 74.1% | 87.3% | 11.8% |
| Verstappen | 10.5% | 52.4% | 87.8% | 11.3% |
| Hamilton | 6.6% | 35.9% | 87.7% | 11.1% |
| Russell | 5.7% | 25.1% | 88.4% | 10.7% |
| Leclerc | 4.1% | 21.0% | 86.2% | 12.8% |
| Piastri | 1.9% | 8.7% | 87.2% | 11.9% |
| Lawson | 0.35% | 1.5% | 81.7% | 15.6% |

Norris vs Antonelli is a coin-flip with a slight edge to the championship leader: pole and dirty-air defence versus the faster Mercedes and a 0.011s qualifying gap. Verstappen’s P3 is sticky if the race stays green; Hamilton/Russell are the cars most likely to break that order under SC. From P8 back, the race is a midfield points fight (Colapinto/Lindblad defending Q3 slots, Gasly the most likely climber from P14, Hulkenberg in the mix). Cadillac and Aston Martin are fighting not to finish last; Stroll’s combination of PU roulette, P22 and 2026 DNF rate is the highest retirement on the grid (~32%).

Expected classified finishers ≈ 18.6 of 22. P1–P11 are essentially always filled; P22 occupancy is only ~2.7% because DNS/NC/DSQ remove cars.

## Principal sources

- Formula 1: Spanish GP event page, qualifying, FP2 report, Bearman FP3 crash, standings and 2026 race results  
- The Race / Crash.net / PlanetF1: full Q1–Q3, starting grid after Sainz and Stroll penalties, FP3 times  
- Sky Sports / Wikipedia: drivers’ and constructors’ standings after Italy; Hadjar/Lawson/Tsunoda substitutions  
- The Race: Italian GP classification (Antonelli 1st from 19th)  
- Pirelli compound note; Coffee Corner Motorsport tyre-allocation and strategy report  
- Driver quotes on overtaking (AP / GPFans / Grande Prêmio)  
- TheSpread.com post-quali winner market (Antonelli +125, Norris +130, Verstappen +600)

# 2026 Spanish Grand Prix (Madring) — pre-race forecast

Round 14 of the 2026 world championship, Sunday 13 September, 57 laps of the new 5.414 km IFEMA Madrid circuit. Forecast is after qualifying and grid penalties, before the race.

## Grid (after penalties)

1 Norris (McLaren) 1:31.824  
2 Antonelli (Mercedes) +0.011  
3 Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.140  
4 Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.189  
5 Leclerc (Ferrari) +0.195  
6 Russell (Mercedes) +0.325  
7 Piastri (McLaren) +0.470  
8 Lawson (Red Bull) +0.492  
9 Colapinto (Alpine) +1.079  
10 Lindblad (Racing Bulls) +1.217  
11 Hulkenberg (Audi)  
12 Bortoleto (Audi)  
13 Ocon (Haas)  
14 Gasly (Alpine)  
15 Tsunoda (Racing Bulls)  
16 Albon (Williams)  
17 Alonso (Aston Martin)  
18 Perez (Cadillac)  
19 Bottas (Cadillac)  
20 Sainz (Williams, 3-place penalty for impeding Bottas)  
21 Bearman (Haas, no Q time after FP3 crash)  
22 Stroll (Aston Martin, 40-place PU penalty; no Q time)

Hadjar sits out a third race with a wrist injury; Lawson remains in the Red Bull, Tsunoda in the Racing Bulls.

## Championship and form

After 13 races (Monza): Antonelli 267, Russell 201, Hamilton 191, Norris 171, Leclerc 155, Verstappen 127, Piastri 116. Mercedes 468–346 over Ferrari in constructors.

Antonelli has seven wins including a 19th-to-first recovery at Monza last weekend. Mercedes swept practice here (Russell FP1, Antonelli FP2/FP3). Norris has won two of the last three Grands Prix (Hungary, Zandvoort) and produced what he called one of his best laps for pole. Ferrari have been Mercedes’ closest match on Friday/Saturday long-run and one-lap pace. Red Bull are a step behind the top three teams; Verstappen still extracted P3. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls occupy the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston Martin’s Honda package has been a reliability and speed disaster; Cadillac (Ferrari customer PU) has 0 points in 13 races.

## Circuit and race character

Madring is a first-time hybrid street/permanent layout: 22 corners, ~340 km/h on the straights, 24% banked “La Monumental”. F3 testing produced 19 red flags. Verstappen and Williams called it a potential “car killer”. Drivers (Antonelli, Russell, Hamilton, Alpine) all said on-track passing is painful — Antonelli spent two practice laps stuck behind a Williams. The run to Turn 1 is only ~200 m, so the start is bunched rather than a long drag.

Weather: dry, air high-20s/low-30s °C, track into the 50s. No rain. Pirelli C2/C3/C4; one-stop medium–hard is the natural call because pit loss plus hard passing punish an extra stop, though Friday graining and a two-stop (M–H–H) remain live. Norris/Antonelli/Verstappen/Russell/Piastri have no new softs; Hamilton and Leclerc kept a fresh C4 as a start/undercut wildcard. Safety-car market was heavily “yes” (~73%).

## Model

120k-race Monte Carlo with:

- Qualifying grid after penalties, plus a small T1 launch mix (Ferrari’s new-soft option, Verstappen’s starts, short run to T1).
- Two finishing-order regimes: a **processional** Plackett–Luce (track position dominates, matching driver feedback) and a **chaos** regime (multiple SCs / red flag / pit lottery) in which Mercedes race pace can still come through, as at Monza.
- Driver-specific mechanical and wall-incident hazards, elevated versus a mature permanent circuit. Extra DNS risk for Bearman (impact-structure rebuild) and Stroll (fresh Honda PU that already leaked water). Small DSQ risk, slightly higher at the front because of plank/skid wear on the banking.
- 90% rule: most DNFs are NC; a minority of late stoppages still classify.

Win probabilities are close to the post-quali market (Antonelli ≈ Norris, then Verstappen, then the Ferraris) but give Russell more win chance than the +2200 board, because the W17 is still the best race car and one SC cycle is enough to use it.

## Headline probabilities

| Driver | P(win) | P(podium) | P(top 10) | P(retirement) |
|--------|--------|-----------|-----------|----------------|
| Antonelli | 36.5% | 79.5% | 89.0% | 10.0% |
| Norris | 33.9% | 74.1% | 87.3% | 11.8% |
| Verstappen | 10.5% | 52.4% | 87.8% | 11.3% |
| Hamilton | 6.6% | 35.9% | 87.7% | 11.1% |
| Russell | 5.7% | 25.1% | 88.4% | 10.7% |
| Leclerc | 4.1% | 21.0% | 86.2% | 12.8% |
| Piastri | 1.9% | 8.7% | 87.2% | 11.9% |
| Lawson | 0.35% | 1.5% | 81.7% | 15.6% |

Norris vs Antonelli is a coin-flip with a slight edge to the championship leader: pole and dirty-air defence versus the faster Mercedes and a 0.011s qualifying gap. Verstappen’s P3 is sticky if the race stays green; Hamilton/Russell are the cars most likely to break that order under SC. From P8 back, the race is a midfield points fight (Colapinto/Lindblad defending Q3 slots, Gasly the most likely climber from P14, Hulkenberg in the mix). Cadillac and Aston Martin are fighting not to finish last; Stroll’s combination of PU roulette, P22 and 2026 DNF rate is the highest retirement on the grid (~32%).

Expected classified finishers ≈ 18.6 of 22. P1–P11 are essentially always filled; P22 occupancy is only ~2.7% because DNS/NC/DSQ remove cars.

import json
pred=json.load(open('/input/prediction.json'))

print('SCORE', json.dumps(score, indent=2))
print()
# print predicted mode/expected vs actual
drivers=pred['drivers']
results={r['driver_id']: r for r in res['results']}
print(f'{\"ID\":4} {\"ACT\":6} {\"P(win)\":8} {\"P(pod)\":8} {\"P(pts)\":8} {\"P(ret)\":8} {\"P(act)\":10} {\"mode\":4} {\"E[pos]\":6}')
for did, d in drivers.items():
    r=results[did]
    pos=r['position']
    act = 'RET' if r['retired'] or r['status']!='classified' else str(pos)
    pwin=d['positions'][0]
    ppod=sum(d['positions'][:3])
    ppts=sum(d['positions'][:10])
    pret=d['retirement']
    if r['retired'] or r['status']=='nc':
        pact=d['nc']
        label='NC'
    elif r['status']=='dns':
        pact=d['dns']
        label='DNS'
    elif r['status']=='dsq':
        pact=d['dsq']
        label='DSQ'
    else:
        pact=d['positions'][pos-1]
        label=str(pos)
    # modal classified position
    mode=max(range(22), key=lambda i: d['positions'][i])+1
    epos=sum((i+1)*p for i,p in enumerate(d['positions'])) / max(sum(d['positions']), 1e-9)
    print(f'{did:4} {act:6} {pwin:8.3f} {ppod:8.3f} {ppts:8.3f} {pret:8.3f} {pact:10.4f} {mode:4} {epos:6.1f}')
"
"}

[[McLaren]]-[[Mercedes AMG High Performance Powertrains|Mercedes]] | Lapchart = {{F1Laps2026|ESP}} }} The '''2026 Spanish Grand Prix''' (officially known as the '''Formula 1 TAG Heuer Gran Premio de España 2026''') was a [[Formula One]] motor race that was held on 13 September 2026, at the [[Madring]] in [[Madrid]], [[Spain]], as the first running of the [[Spanish Grand Prix]] at the recently-constructed Madring track. It was the fourteenth round of the [[2026 Formula One World Championship]]. [[Lando Norris]] ([[McLaren]]) took pole position for the race, but lost out to [[Kimi Antonelli]] ([[Mercedes-Benz in Formula One|Mercedes]]). [[Max Verstappen]] ([[Red Bull Racing|Red Bull]]) completed the podium alongside Norris. ==Background== The event was held at the [[Madring]] in [[Madrid]] for the first time in the circuit's history, and for the first time as a host for the [[Spanish Grand Prix]], across the weekend of 11–13 September.{{cite web |title=Madrid |url=https://www.statsf1.com/en/circuit-madrid.aspx |website=StatsF1.com |access-date=7 September 2026}} The most recent venue to hold the Spanish Grand Prix was the [[Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya]] at [[Montmeló]], Spain, which currently hosts the [[Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix]] on rotation with the [[Belgian Grand Prix]]. The Grand Prix was the fourteenth round of the [[2026 Formula One World Championship]] and the 56th running of the Spanish Grand Prix as a round of the Formula One World Championship.{{cite web |title=Grands Prix Spain|url=https://www.statsf1.com/en/grand-prix-spain.aspx |website=StatsF1.com |access-date=7 September 2026}} ===Championship standings before the race=== Going into the weekend, [[Kimi Antonelli]] led the [[List of Formula One World Drivers' Champions|Drivers' Championship]] with 267 points, 66 points ahead of teammate [[George Russell (racing driver)|George Russell]] in second and 76 ahead of [[Lewis Hamilton]] in third. [[Mercedes-Benz in Formula One|Mercedes]], with 468 points, led the [[World Constructors' Championship|Constructors' Championship]] from [[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]] and [[McLaren]], who were second and third with 346 and 287 points, respectively.{{cite web|url=https://www.statsf1.com/en/2026/pays-bas/championnat.aspx|title=Italy 2026 – Championship|website=Stats F1|date=6 September 2026|access-date=6 September 2026}} ===Entrants=== {{See also|2026 Formula One World Championship#Entries}} The drivers and teams were the same as published in the season entry list, with the exception of [[Isack Hadjar]] at [[Red Bull Racing|Red Bull]], who injured his wrist leading into the [[2026 Dutch Grand Prix|Dutch Grand Prix]] and was again unable to compete. Like the previous two Grands Prix, he was again replaced by [[Liam Lawson]]. recently-constructed Madring track. It was the fourteenth round of the [[2026 Formula One World Championship]]. [[Lando Norris]] ([[McLaren]]) took pole position for the race, but lost out to [[Kimi Antonelli]] ([[Mercedes-Benz in Formula One|Mercedes]]). [[Max Verstappen]] ([[Red Bull Racing|Red Bull]]) completed the podium alongside Norris. ==Background== The event was held at the [[Madring]] in [[Madrid]] for the first time in the circuit's history, and for the first time as a host for the [[Spanish Grand Prix]], across the weekend of 11–13 September.{{cite web |title=Madrid |url=https://www.statsf1.com/en/circuit-madrid.aspx |website=StatsF1.com |access-date=7 September 2026}} The most recent venue to hold the Spanish Grand Prix was the [[Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya]] at [[Montmeló]], Spain, which currently hosts the [[Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix]] on rotation with the [[Belgian Grand Prix]]. The Grand Prix was the fourteenth round of the [[2026 Formula One World Championship]] and the 56th running of the Spanish Grand Prix as a round of the Formula One World Championship.{{cite web |title=Grands Prix Spain|url=https://www.statsf1.com/en/grand-prix-spain.aspx |website=StatsF1.com |access-date=7 September 2026}} ===Championship standings before the race=== Going into the weekend, [[Kimi Antonelli]] led the [[List of Formula One World Drivers' Champions|Drivers' Championship]] with 267 points, 66 points ahead of teammate [[George Russell (racing driver)|George Russell]] in second and 76 ahead of [[Lewis Hamilton]] in third. [[Mercedes-Benz in Formula One|Mercedes]], with 468 points, led the [[World Constructors' Championship|Constructors' Championship]] from [[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]] and [[McLaren]], who were second and third with 346 and 287 points, respectively.{{cite web|url=https://www.statsf1.com/en/2026/pays-bas/championnat.aspx|title=Italy 2026 – Championship|website=Stats F1|date=6 September 2026|access-date=6 September 2026}} ===Entrants=== {{See also|2026 Formula One World Championship#Entries}} The drivers and teams were the same as published in the season entry list, with the exception of [[Isack Hadjar]] at [[Red Bull Racing|Red Bull]], who injured his wrist leading into the [[2026 Dutch Grand Prix|Dutch Grand Prix]] and was again unable to compete. Like the previous two Grands Prix, he was again replaced by [[Liam Lawson]]. Red Bull reserve driver [[Yuki Tsunoda]] replaced Lawson at [[Racing Bulls]].{{Cite web |last=Holter |first=Felix |last2=Corsmit |first2=Natalie |last3=Remmerie |first3=Mathieu |last4=Warwick |first4=Derek |author-link4=Derek Warwick |last5=Domingo |first5=David |date=11 September 2026 |title=2026 Spanish Grand Prix – Entry List |url=https://www.fia.com/system/files/decision-document/2026_spanish_grand_prix_-_entry_list.pdf |access-date=11 September 2026 |publisher=[[Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile]]}}{{cite web|url=https://www.motorsport.com/f1/news/isack-hadjar-to-sit-out-third-f1-race-in-madrid-as-yuki-tsunoda-returns/10853531/|title=Isack Hadjar to sit out third F1 race in Madrid as Yuki Tsunoda returns|publisher=Motorsport.com|date=7 September 2026|access-date=7 September 2026}} === Tyre choices === {{further|Formula One tyres}} Tyre supplier [[Pirelli]] selected its C2, C3, and C4 compounds—the middle three in its range—for the event, designating them as hard, medium, and soft, respectively.{{cite web|url=https://press.pirelli.com/the-madring-makes-its-world-championship-debut-with-the-challenge-of-the-monumental/|title=The Madring makes its World Championship debut with the challenge of the "Monumental"|publisher=Pirelli.com|date=8 September 2026|access-date=8 September 2026}} == Practice == Three free [[Formula One racing#Free practice|practice sessions]] were held for the event. The first free practice session was held on 11 September 2026, at 13:30 local time ([[UTC+2]]), and was topped by [[George Russell (racing driver)|George Russell]] ([[Mercedes-Benz in Formula One|Mercedes]]) ahead of his teammate [[Kimi Antonelli]] and [[Charles Leclerc]] ([[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]]). The second free practice session was held on the same day, at 17:00 local time, and was topped by Antonelli ahead of Leclerc and his teammate [[Lewis Hamilton]]. A red flag was observed due to [[Arvid Lindblad]] ([[Racing Bulls]]) hitting the wall at turn 13. The third free practice session was held on 12 September 2026, at 12:30 local time, and was topped by Antonelli ahead of Leclerc and [[Oscar Piastri]] ([[McLaren]]). Sep 14, 2026 9:22am UTC Oscar Piastri had a race to forget in Madrid after a first lap incident derailed his afternoon on a day where Lando Norris showed the McLaren had the pace to fight for the win. The Australian finished down in eighth place, behind the Alpine of Franco Colapinto, and while the unlucky timing of the Virtual Safety Car prevented his team mate from fighting for the win, Piastri had his own slice of misfortune. He picked up damage to his front wing after first lap contact with George Russell’s Mercedes, with the Australian left nowhere to go as the Mercedes ducked across the track towards the barriers. That left him with aero damage in the form of a broken end-plate and short on downforce, something the team could only mitigate but not fully fix at his one and only pit stop. And having started on the hard tyres, the timing of the early Virtual Safety Car also proved problematic for the 25-year-old. “It was pretty painful obviously, from Lap 1," he assessed afterwards. "Yeah, not much I really could have done from there. "The timing for the VSC was certainly not ideal for us, [stayed] on the hard and it was just a difficult afternoon." Having opted not to stop under the VSC, Piastri ran a long opening stint in the hopes of a later VSC, Safety Car or red flag moment. But no more incidents came, leaving him to make a pit stop under full racing conditions. The time lost meant he came out in traffic and, while he pulled off one of the few overtakes on Sunday, picking off Arvid Lindblad , Piastri could not find a way past the Alpine of Colapinto late on. To trace back the difficulties Piastri faced, you have to look to Qualifying where he needed an extra set of softs to guarantee he made it through Q2. That left him as the only front runner to have a used set of the C4 tyre for his first run in Q3. On his second run on the new tyres, where balance would have been different to the used set, he made a mistake early in his lap and from there, could only qualify seventh. That left him starting in the midst of the pack, something always fraught with danger as all the cars barrel down into Turn 1 on a narrow street track. Piastri was left with a damaged car for the entirety of the Madrid race “It was mostly the end of Qualifying and then Lap 1 obviously was far from ideal, having damage for the whole race,” he explained. “It was tough like that, but today we just tried to learn as much as we could to try and get more out of the car and the way I drive it. Hopefully we’ve learned a few things for the rest of the year.” Piastri has two podiums to show for his 2026 season, the last of which came in Miami, and one top-three finish in a Sprint. His team mate has five rostrums, including two victories, a Sprint win, three other Sprint top-three finishes, three pole positions and a Sprint pole. The contrast between their two seasons is stark, and is further highlighted in the Championship where Norris has amassed 66 more points than his team mate. Piastri will be hoping his luck changes soon, and he has a chance to set things right next time out in Azerbaijan. Red Bull Max Verstappen cut the corner at Turn 2 when fighting with Hamilton, and was even briefly ahead of Antonelli. But the team told him to give the positions back, which after Hamilton retired left him third. The Dutchman benefitted from a VSC pit stop to jump ahead of Norris, and managed to catch Antonelli to show the RB22 had some good race pace. He kept a charging Norris at bay in the closing stages for his second straight rostrum. As for Liam Lawson , he ran a long stint on the hards, and had to fight hard to come home sixth. He could not keep a fresher shod Russell at bay, but did manage to overtake Gasly before a lonely end to his race. Max Verstappen, 2nd “It was a great result, and we really maximised our performance, with finishing P2 on this track a solid way to wrap up a good weekend. At the start, Lewis clipped the kerb and jumped back onto the racing line, I had to go off track, otherwise both of us would have taken damage. I don't think we had the pace to challenge for the lead anyway, Kimi and Lando were faster than me throughout, so I'm happy with second. It's a circuit that's very difficult to pass on; if you position yourself in the middle, there isn't really a way through, so I was able to hold off Lando until the end. This double header has been a positive one. The car has been in a decent window both weekends, and we've been able to score consistently good points over the last few races. A podium is a nice way to end the European swing." Liam Lawson, 6th "I think it was a decent race. We had good speed through parts of it, but I just think we weren’t on the ideal strategy today. We went for the alternate strategy, starting on the Hards. At the start I lost the position to Franco and lost a lot of time as it was, but by the time I cleared him the VSC came out and they’d boxed, so it was just tricky from there. The start was exciting and I had to take a lot of risks to get the move done on Franco because it’s quite difficult to overtake here. It would’ve been nice to start a bit higher, but considering where we did start, the result today was good and I’m happy we managed to gain two places in the Race. I’m much more confident in the car this week, we’ve made a couple of great steps, so there are some good things to take away from the weekend." Laurent Mekies, Team Principal “After Monza another strong result from the whole Team at the end of a tough race. Once again, Max extracted absolutely everything from the car, as he always does. There was obviously some frustration at the start when he had to give the place back to Lewis, but the Team on the pit wall took a good look at it and, credit to them, made the difficult call. It was painful at the time, but Max immediately got himself back into the fight and was outstanding all the way to the flag, including a great defence against the McLaren in the final laps. "It was also a strong race and some good points from Liam. It certainly wasn’t easy towards the end of his first stint on worn Hard tyres, but he kept his cool and showed good pace in the final stint. "Max’s P2 is his fifth podium in the last seven races and, although we have had a couple of tricky moments along the way, we are continuing to close the gap and credit needs to go to everyone working behind the scenes at Milton Keynes, improving every aspect of the car and its PU.” MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 13: Race winner Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy and Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team and Second placed Max Verstappen of the Netherlands and Oracle Red Bull Racing celebrate on the podium with Champagne during the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 13, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images) Previous image 0/2 Next image McLaren Lando Norris had a great start from pole and after some early shenanigans with track limits, settled into the lead. He built a decent gap to Antonelli behind but when a VSC was called he was already past the pit lane entry. As such, Antonelli and Verstappen behind pitted for a cheap stop. By the time Norris came around, the VSC had ended – and then he had a slow pit stop to boot, which dropped him down the order. The reigning World Champion did well to fight back to the podium, but luck was not on his side today. Nor was it on Oscar Piastri ’s, who suffered front wing damage after being squeezed by Russell off the line. That dropped him out of the top 10, but he ran a long first stint to fight back, and pulled off some overtakes to at least finish in the points. Qualifying was perfect, the race in terms of performance was perfect, and we were quickest by a big margin. It's just incredibly frustrating to lose in a way that has nothing to do with performance. It’s disappointing, especially considering all the effort that went into the weekend both here at the track and back at the factory. We will turn our attention to the next race and do our best to come back strong there." Charles Leclerc, 4th "The race was good and we brought home what was realistically the best result possible, given that this track is so difficult to overtake on. As for Lewis, at this stage we don’t yet know the exact cause of the brake system issue that forced him to retire and we will investigate it thoroughly. Regarding the championship, our approach remains the same: we take it one race at a time, and our focus now turns to Baku." Audi Audi managed to get one car home in the points after running different strategies out there. Nico Hulkenberg started on the softs, and pitted under the VSC which made his race. He climbed to P10, for his third score of the year. Gabriel Bortoleto started on the hards and hung it out in the hopes of a Safety Car. That never came, and he dropped out of the top 10 after eventually pitting, the Brazilian also handed a warning for moving under braking. Nico Hulkenberg, 10th "We got the maximum out of what we had today. Starting on the soft tyre meant the early Virtual Safety Car was the right window for us to pit, and the pit crew did a fantastic job to get me ahead of Esteban [Ocon]. That was probably the key moment of our race because it gave us the track position we needed. From there, it was all about managing the tyres. Overtaking was very difficult with everyone running at a similar pace, so there wasn't much room to make further progress. We've been towards the top of this midfield fight for a while now, hopefully we will soon make the extra step we need to keep moving forward." Gabriel Bortoleto, 13th “We got unlucky with the Virtual Safety Car today, which pretty much messed up with our plans, and after that nothing else happened until the end of the race - not much more we could have done from there, especially as chances to overtake were slim. “Overall, it's been a weekend of learnings. It wasn’t the best, but it was not all that bad either, and I have quite enjoyed racing around here. In qualifying, we were close to making it into Q3 again, and that was more or less where our pace has been all weekend. Now, a week to recharge and get back to work before we head to Baku in two weeks.” Allan McNish, Racing Director “Overall, we’re happy to have gained a point. It was always going to be a difficult race from a strategy point of view, with overtaking being very difficult and it looking strongly like a one-stop race. We dropped positions again at the start, which is an area we know is one of our weaknesses, but from there I was very pleased with how we worked as a team. “We played a real team game today. Nico switched from the soft onto the hard tyre, while we ran an alternative strategy with Gabi which covered pretty much every scenario. Gabi did a great job to run very long on the hard, with the hope that a Safety Car, Virtual Safety Car or red flag later in the race could give him a significant tyre advantage, or a free stop, and propel him back into the points. On the other side, Nico was very strong on both the soft and the hard and came very close to getting ahead of Lindblad at the end. “Ultimately, I have to say the point today was delivered by the team in the pits. Nico came in behind Ocon and went out ahead of him after a fantastically quick stop, and the team repeated that performance when Gabi came in. It was a very good team effort, strategically, in the pits and from both drivers. It’s another point for us, and now we look forward to Baku.” MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 13: Nico Hulkenberg of Germany driving the (27) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at Madring on September 13, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. The race recap shows a classic street-circuit grind where the VSC timing created the real story, not the usual overtaking battles. Hamilton’s early brake failure and Leclerc’s late pit stop both highlight how fragile the strategy can be when the race stays processional. The two-stoppers like Russell and the damage-affected drivers like 8th-placed Piastri also fit the expected pattern of hard-tyre dominance.

Looking at the forecast misses, Hamilton’s retirement stands out as the clearest systematic error. The 11.1 % probability was reasonable, but the model underestimated the severity of his FP3 wall impact and the rebuild time needed. That’s 10 % mechanical luck that should have been baked into the front-runner DNF rate for rebuilt cars on high-brake-stress tracks. The Norris P3 outcome was more randomness than model failure—VSC timing is inherently unpredictable, and the forecast already captured the chaos regime correctly.

The biggest reusable lesson is that overnight repairs after 3rd-practice incidents raise brake and cooling risk far more than generic DNF rates suggest. On street circuits, lap-1 pack contact from midfield starters also creates a heavier left tail in position distributions than the model currently weights. import json, math
pred=json.load(open('/input/prediction.json'))
res=json.load(open('/input/result.json'))
results={r['driver_id']: r for r in res['results']}

print("=== log loss by driver ===")
rows=[]
for did,d in pred['drivers'].items():
    r=results[did]
    if r['status']=='nc' or r['retired']:
        p=d['nc']; act='NC'
    elif r['status']=='dns':
        p=d['dns']; act='DNS'
    elif r['status']=='dsq':
        p=d['dsq']; act='DSQ'
    else:
        p=d['positions'][r['position']-1]; act=str(r['position'])
    p=max(p,1e-12)
    ll=-math.log(p)
    # rank error if classified
    epos=sum((i+1)*x for i,x in enumerate(d['positions']))/max(sum(d['positions']),1e-9)
    if r['position']:
        mae=abs(r['position']-epos)
    else:
        mae=None
    pret=d['retirement']
    ret_err=(1 if r['retired'] else 0)-pret
    rows.append((ll, did, act, p, epos, mae, pret, ret_err))
rows.sort(reverse=True)
print(f"{'LL':6} {'ID':4} {'ACT':4} {'p':8} {'Epos':6} {'MAE':6} {'Pret':6} {'ret_err':7}")
for ll,did,act,p,epos,mae,pret,re in rows:
    mae_s=f"{mae:.2f}" if mae is not None else "NA"
    print(f"{ll:6.3f} {did:4} {act:4} {p:8.4f} {epos:6.2f} {mae_s:6} {pret:6.3f} {re:+7.3f}")

print("\nmean ll", sum(r[0] for r in rows)/len(rows))

# win/podium/points brier components
print("\n=== event briers ===")
for did,d in pred['drivers'].items():
    r=results[did]
    win=1 if r['position']==1 else 0
    pod=1 if r['position'] and r['position']<=3 else 0
    pts=1 if r['position'] and r['position']<=10 else 0
    ret=1 if r['retired'] else 0
    pwin=d['positions'][0]
    ppod=sum(d['positions'][:3])
    ppts=sum(d['positions'][:10])
    pret=d['retirement']
    print(f"{did} winB={(pwin-win)**2:.4f} podB={(ppod-pod)**2:.4f} ptsB={(ppts-pts)**2:.4f} retB={(pret-ret)**2:.4f}  act w/p/t/r={win,pod,pts,ret}")

# classified count
n_class=sum(1 for r in res['results'] if r['status']=='classified')
print("classified", n_class)

# cumulative P mass at actual for classified
print("\nGrid vs finish deltas")
grid={"NOR":1,"ANT":2,"VER":3,"HAM":4,"LEC":5,"RUS":6,"PIA":7,"LAW":8,"COL":9,"LIN":10,"HUL":11,"BOR":12,"OCO":13,"GAS":14,"TSU":15,"ALB":16,"ALO":17,"PER":18,"BOT":19,"SAI":20,"STR":21,"BEA":99}
# bearman PL
for r in res['results']:
    g=grid[r['driver_id']]
    fin=r['position'] if r['position'] else 'NC'
    delta = (g-fin) if isinstance(fin,int) and g<90 else None
    print(f"{r['driver_id']:4} grid {g:3} -> {fin} delta={delta}")

pred=json.load(open('/input/prediction.json'))
res=json.load(open('/input/result.json'))
results={r['driver_id']: r for r in res['results']}

print("=== log loss by driver ===")
rows=[]
for did,d in pred['drivers'].items():
    r=results[did]
    if r['status']=='nc' or r['retired']:
        p=d['nc']; act='NC'
    elif r['status']=='dns':
        p=d['dns']; act='DNS'
    elif r['status']=='dsq':
        p=d['dsq']; act='DSQ'
    else:
        p=d['positions'][r['position']-1]; act=str(r['position'])
    p=max(p,1e-12)
    ll=-math.log(p)
    # rank error if classified
    epos=sum((i+1)*x for i,x in enumerate(d['positions']))/max(sum(d['positions']),1e-9)
    if r['position']:
        mae=abs(r['position']-epos)
    else:
        mae=None
    pret=d['retirement']
    ret_err=(1 if r['retired'] else 0)-pret
    rows.append((ll, did, act, p, epos, mae, pret, ret_err))
rows.sort(reverse=True)
print(f"{'LL':6} {'ID':4} {'ACT':4} {'p':8} {'Epos':6} {'MAE':6} {'Pret':6} {'ret_err':7}")
for ll,did,act,p,epos,mae,pret,re in rows:
    mae_s=f"{mae:.2f}" if mae is not None else "NA"
    print(f"{ll:6.3f} {did:4} {act:4} {p:8.4f} {epos:6.2f} {mae_s:6} {pret:6.3f} {re:+7.3f}")

print("\nmean ll", sum(r[0] for r in rows)/len(rows))

# win/podium/points brier components
print("\n=== event briers ===")
for did,d in pred['drivers'].items():
    r=results[did]
    win=1 if r['position']==1 else 0
    pod=1 if r['position'] and r['position']<=3 else 0
    pts=1 if r['position'] and r['position']<=10 else 0
    ret=1 if r['retired'] else 0
    pwin=d['positions'][0]
    ppod=sum(d['positions'][:3])
    ppts=sum(d['positions'][:10])
    pret=d['retirement']

# classified count
n_class=sum(1 for r in res['results'] if r['status']=='classified')
print("classified", n_class)

# cumulative P mass at actual for classified
print("\nGrid vs finish deltas")
grid={"NOR":1,"ANT":2,"VER":3,"HAM":4,"LEC":5,"RUS":6,"PIA":7,"LAW":8,"COL":9,"LIN":10,"HUL":11,"BOR":12,"OCO":13,"GAS":14,"TSU":15,"ALB":16,"ALO":17,"PER":18,"BOT":19,"SAI":20,"STR":21,"BEA":99}
# bearman PL
for r in res['results']:
    g=grid[r['driver_id']]
    fin=r['position'] if r['position'] else 'NC'
    delta = (g-fin) if isinstance(fin,int) and g<90 else None
    print(f"{r['driver_id']:4} grid {g:3} -> {fin} delta={delta}")
PY
"}

{"command":"cat > /memory/notes.md << 'EOF'
# Forecast notes

## 2026 snapshot (through Rd 14 Madrid)

Drivers: ANT 292, RUS 211, HAM 191, NOR 186, LEC 167, VER 145, PIA 120.
Constructors: Mercedes 503, Ferrari 358, McLaren 306, Red Bull 230, Racing Bulls 77, Alpine 68.
Winners: ANT x8 (CHN, JPN, MIA, CAN, MON, BEL, ITA from P19, ESP), RUS x2, NOR x2, HAM (BCN), LEC (GBR).
Line-up: Hadjar (RB) still out wrist — Lawson in RB, Tsunoda in Racing Bulls (NED/ITA/ESP). Cadillac 0 pts. Aston Honda still a reliability/speed disaster. Next: Baku (Rd 15).

## Madrid (Rd 14) result vs forecast — what to keep vs discard

Result: ANT, VER, NOR, LEC, RUS, LAW, COL, PIA, LIN, HUL | OCO, GAS, BOR, TSU, ALB, BEA, ALO, BOT. NC: HAM (brakes, lap 6), STR (brakes after damage, lap 12), PER (water/PU, lap 31), SAI (collision damage, lap 43). 18 classified vs E≈18.6.

Keep: ANT 36.5% win / NOR 33.9% was the right coin-flip (market +125/+130). Win Brier 0.024, podium Brier 0.026. Midfield almost grid-locked (P9–P18 moved 0 to +2). Processional prior was correct. Stroll highest DNF (~32%) hit. Cadillac/Aston at the back hit. One-stop + hard-to-pass character hit.

Do not overfit: VSC stealing Norris’s win; HAM’s first DNF of the year; Piastri’s T1 wing; F3’s 19 red flags (F1 had one VSC, no SC, no red). Do not bump ANT’s base rate just because he won; do not treat pole as a curse.

## Reusable modeling lessons

### 1. Three interruption regimes, not two
Madrid model mixed (a) green Plackett–Luce and (b) multi-SC/red-flag chaos. The race was a third, more common, modern-F1 state: **a single VSC that is a pit-phase lottery without enabling on-track reordering**.

- Leader who has just passed pit entry cannot stop; P2/P3 can take a cheap stop and jump them. That decided ANT vs NOR. VER also boxed under VSC → P2.
- Cars that park in a runoff gap (Stroll) often produce a **VSC, not a full SC**. Support-series red-flag counts overstate F1 red-flag/SC probability on a new circuit.
- On a no-overtake track, one VSC is enough to decide the win and still leave the rest of the field processional. Chaos-regime mass that lets “best race car from P6” win needs a full SC/red, which did not occur (RUS stayed P5).

Action: add an explicit **single-neutralization pit-lottery** regime. On processional tracks, shave leader win probability toward P2 whenever pit loss is large. Do not let F2/F3 red-flag counts dominate F1 SC/red priors.

### 2. Starting compound × interruption timing is first-order
Early VSC helped cars that **wanted** to stop soon (medium/soft one-stop: ANT, VER, HUL, COL). It hurt hard-tyre long-stint cars (LEC, RUS, PIA, LAW, GAS, BOR) who needed a *late* SC/red.

- LEC led ~32 laps on hards waiting for a late SC/red; pitted lap 48 → P4 (would have been P4 on the other strategy too).
- RUS: hard start, VSC onto mediums, second stop to hard → still P5. Overtaking dead, strategy could not pass LEC.
- GAS/BOR hung out to the end; no late incident → out of points.

Action: do not give generic “climber” points mass from P12–P16 on a processional track unless an interruption is likely *and* timed for their compound. Split-strategy value is timing-dependent, not a free “chaos overlay”.

### 3. Overnight rebuilds and thermal street-circuit DNFs
HAM: FP3 wall at T22, rebuilt overnight, Q4, superb launch, then brake-pedal failure (first DNF of his season). Forecast used a generic ~11% front-runner retirement — same as NOR/VER — and paid for it in retirement/points Brier.

STR also brakes (after early damage) in heat. Bottas spent the race managing brake temps. PER water-pressure/PU. Track into the 50s °C, heavy braking, long straights, banking.

Action:
- After an FP crash/rebuild, bump **mechanical** DNF (brakes, cooling, hydraulics, floor), not only DNS. The car that starts is not a healthy car.
- On hot, heavy-braking street circuits, elevate **brake/cooling/PU thermal** DNF vs “wall hit” DNF. Driver “car killer” quotes overstated *full-course* chaos; they were closer to right on *component* stress.
- Do not apply a uniform ~10–12% DNF to every top-10 car. Rebuild, new PU, and thermal-street flags should differentiate.

Field DNF count was fine (4 vs ~3.4). The miss was **who** DNFed (a P4 Ferrari), not the total.

### 4. Pack-start damage is sticky when passing is dead
Processional Plackett–Luce perturbs order; it understates “broken wing/floor on lap 1 → finish several places down with almost no recovery”.

- PIA: P7, squeezed by RUS, broken endplate, only stop couldn’t fix it, P8. Biggest position log-loss. P(top 10) was fine; the **place distribution was too peaked** around P5–P7.
- TSU: Sainz T1 contact, damaged, P14.
- SAI: T1 lockup vs TSU, later hit ALO, retired with damage.
- STR: opening-lap damage then brakes.

Action: on no-overtake layouts, give P6–P12 a fatter left tail (damage → +3–6 places lost, or NC). Pit-lane starters (BEA) also have little climb without a full SC; P16 from PL is typical, not a points tail.

### 5. Grid still dominates the midfield on this circuit type
COL 9→7, LIN 10→9, HUL 11→10, OCO 13→11, GAS 14→12, BOR 12→13, TSU 15→14, ALB 16→15, ALO 17→17, BOT 19→18. HAM’s early DNF was the main +1 shuffle.

Keep a strong track-position model from ~P8 back. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls are the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston/Cadillac fighting not to be last. Q3 slots (COL, LIN) converting to points is the default if they finish.

GAS as “most likely climber from P14” was the main midfield over-credit. Without a late SC, P14 on a processional track stays ~P12–P14.

### 6. Quali gap of 0.01s: prefer the better race car / championship leader
ANT from P2 beat polesitter after a VSC, but also had genuine Mercedes race pace and FP lockout. NOR was fastest in the race until the VSC; both belong in the high-30s win range when the gap is 0.011s. Do not collapse them to 50/50 on pole alone, and do not treat the VSC outcome as evidence NOR was mis-ranked.

VER P3 is sticky on a processional track if he finishes (here P2 via VSC + HAM DNF). He still could not match ANT/NOR on pace — “best of the rest” remains the Red Bull base.

### 7. Friday compound reading vs Sunday
Pirelli: C2 hard was little-run on Friday and was the race tyre (stints >45 laps). Medium/soft grained but were usable. Teams that over-indexed Friday long runs, or assumed two-stop from graining, were wrong.

Action: on a new street circuit, treat Friday tyre conclusions as weak. High pit loss + no passing makes one-stop the default even if Friday said otherwise. Hard can be the race tyre without Friday evidence.

### 8. Constructor reliability priors (do not shrink yet)
- Aston–Honda: still DNF-prone (STR) and slow (ALO P17). High retirement, near-zero points until the package actually scores.
- Cadillac–Ferrari PU: PER water/PU DNF, BOT last classified, 0 points in 14 races. Keep high DNF, negligible points.
- Williams: no pace (ALB “best we could hope”: beat Astons + one Haas). Points only via chaos.
- Audi: HUL P10 via VSC pit-stop vs OCO. Midfield points are a pit-execution / compound-timing thing, not race-pace overtake.

## Circuit-type flags for later rounds

- **No-overtake street / short T1 run** (Madrid, Monaco, Hungary-like): processional + VSC pit lottery; pack-damage sticky; climber narratives are SC-timed only.
- **Long-straight street** (Baku, Singapore, Jeddah): do **not** copy Madrid’s zero-overtake prior. Baku historically has real passing on the main straight **and** a high genuine SC rate (walls, debris). Use higher SC/red mass than Madrid, and allow more on-track reordering than Plackett–Luce-from-grid.
- **Hot + heavy braking**: extra brake/cooling/PU DNF, especially rebuilt cars and weak-cooling teams.
- Next is Baku: upgrades mentioned for Williams; Aston weight-saving; triple-header starts. Lawson/Tsunoda/Hadjar status TBD. ANT lead now 81 pts.

## Calibration targets
Headline win/podium were good. Spend effort on (1) front-runner DNF heterogeneity, (2) VSC-vs-SC-vs-red mixture, (3) fatter incident tails for pack starters on processional tracks, (4) compound–timing interaction. Do not retune midfield means that were already within ~1 place.
EOF
echo "wrote notes, wc:"; wc -l /memory/notes.md
"}

Early VSC helped cars that **wanted** to stop soon (medium/soft one-stop: ANT, VER, HUL, COL). It hurt hard-tyre long-stint cars (LEC, RUS, PIA, LAW, GAS, BOR) who needed a *late* SC/red.

- LEC led ~32 laps on hards waiting for a late SC/red; pitted lap 48 → P4 (would have been P4 on the other strategy too).
- RUS: hard start, VSC onto mediums, second stop to hard → still P5. Overtaking dead, strategy could not pass LEC.
- GAS/BOR hung out to the end; no late incident → out of points.

Action: do not give generic “climber” points mass from P12–P16 on a processional track unless an interruption is likely *and* timed for their compound. Split-strategy value is timing-dependent, not a free “chaos overlay”.

### 3. Overnight rebuilds and thermal street-circuit DNFs
HAM: FP3 wall at T22, rebuilt overnight, Q4, superb launch, then brake-pedal failure (first DNF of his season). Forecast used a generic ~11% front-runner retirement — same as NOR/VER — and paid for it in retirement/points Brier.

STR also brakes (after early damage) in heat. Bottas spent the race managing brake temps. PER water-pressure/PU. Track into the 50s °C, heavy braking, long straights, banking.

Action:
- After an FP crash/rebuild, bump **mechanical** DNF (brakes, cooling, hydraulics, floor), not only DNS. The car that starts is not a healthy car.
- On hot, heavy-braking street circuits, elevate **brake/cooling/PU thermal** DNF vs “wall hit” DNF. Driver “car killer” quotes overstated *full-course* chaos; they were closer to right on *component* stress.
- Do not apply a uniform ~10–12% DNF to every top-10 car. Rebuild, new PU, and thermal-street flags should differentiate.

Field DNF count was fine (4 vs ~3.4). The miss was **who** DNFed (a P4 Ferrari), not the total.

### 4. Pack-start damage is sticky when passing is dead
Processional Plackett–Luce perturbs order; it understates “broken wing/floor on lap 1 → finish several places down with almost no recovery”.

- PIA: P7, squeezed by RUS, broken endplate, only stop couldn’t fix it, P8. Biggest position log-loss. P(top 10) was fine; the **place distribution was too peaked** around P5–P7.
- TSU: Sainz T1 contact, damaged, P14.
- SAI: T1 lockup vs TSU, later hit ALO, retired with damage.
- STR: opening-lap damage then brakes.

Action: on no-overtake layouts, give P6–P12 a fatter left tail (damage → +3–6 places lost, or NC). Pit-lane starters (BEA) also have little climb without a full SC; P16 from PL is typical, not a points tail.

### 5. Grid still dominates the midfield on this circuit type
COL 9→7, LIN 10→9, HUL 11→10, OCO 13→11, GAS 14→12, BOR 12→13, TSU 15→14, ALB 16→15, ALO 17→17, BOT 19→18. HAM’s early DNF was the main +1 shuffle.

Keep a strong track-position model from ~P8 back. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls are the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston/Cadillac fighting not to be last. Q3 slots (COL, LIN) converting to points is the default if they finish.

GAS as “most likely climber from P14” was the main midfield over-credit. Without a late SC, P14 on a processional track stays ~P12–P14.

### 6. Quali gap of 0.01s: prefer the better race car / championship leader
ANT from P2 beat polesitter after a VSC, but also had genuine Mercedes race pace and FP lockout. NOR was fastest in the race until the VSC; both belong in the high-30s win range when the gap is 0.011s. Do not collapse them to 50/50 on pole alone, and do not treat the VSC outcome as evidence NOR was mis-ranked.

VER P3 is sticky on a processional track if he finishes (here P2 via VSC + HAM DNF). He still could not match ANT/NOR on pace — “best of the rest” remains the Red Bull base.

### 7. Friday compound reading vs Sunday
Pirelli: C2 hard was little-run on Friday and was the race tyre (stints >45 laps). Medium/soft grained but were usable. Teams that over-indexed Friday long runs, or assumed two-stop from graining, were wrong.

Action: on a new street circuit, treat Friday tyre conclusions as weak. High pit loss + no passing makes one-stop the default even if Friday said otherwise. Hard can be the race tyre without Friday evidence.

### 8. Constructor reliability priors (do not shrink yet)
- Aston–Honda: still DNF-prone (STR) and slow (ALO P17). High retirement, near-zero points until the package actually scores.
- Cadillac–Ferrari PU: PER water/PU DNF, BOT last classified, 0 points in 14 races. Keep high DNF, negligible points.
- Williams: no pace (ALB “best we could hope”: beat Astons + one Haas). Points only via chaos.
- Audi: HUL P10 via VSC pit-stop vs OCO. Midfield points are a pit-execution / compound-timing thing, not race-pace overtake.

## Circuit-type flags for later rounds

- **No-overtake street / short T1 run** (Madrid, Monaco, Hungary-like): processional + VSC pit lottery; pack-damage sticky; climber narratives are SC-timed only.
- **Long-straight street** (Baku, Singapore, Jeddah): do **not** copy Madrid’s zero-overtake prior. Baku historically has real passing on the main straight **and** a high genuine SC rate (walls, debris). Use higher SC/red mass than Madrid, and allow more on-track reordering than Plackett–Luce-from-grid.
- **Hot + heavy braking**: extra brake/cooling/PU DNF, especially rebuilt cars and weak-cooling teams.
- Next is Baku: upgrades mentioned for Williams; Aston weight-saving; triple-header starts. Lawson/Tsunoda/Hadjar status TBD. ANT lead now 81 pts.

## Calibration targets
Headline win/podium were good. Spend effort on (1) front-runner DNF heterogeneity, (2) VSC-vs-SC-vs-red mixture, (3) fatter incident tails for pack starters on processional tracks, (4) compound–timing interaction. Do not retune midfield means that were already within ~1 place.
